Guideline: Register Compositions with Explicit Metadata
Description: Every video must be registered via <Composition> inside RemotionRoot with explicit id, durationInFrames, fps, width, and height. Remotion cannot infer video length or dimensions from CSS or component render output the way a browser page can.
Do: Set durationInFrames, fps, width, height explicitly on every <Composition>
Don't: Omit dimensions or duration and expect Remotion to infer them from rendered DOM size
Code Good: <Composition id="MyVideo" component={MyVideo} durationInFrames={150} fps={30} width={1920} height={1080} />
Code Bad: <Composition id="MyVideo" component={MyVideo} /> // missing fps/duration/dimensions — registration throws

Guideline: durationInFrames Equals fps Times Seconds
Description: durationInFrames is a frame count, not milliseconds or seconds. Compute it as fps * desiredSeconds so the video length stays correct if fps changes later.
Do: Derive durationInFrames from fps and a seconds constant
Don't: Hardcode an arbitrary frame count disconnected from fps
Code Good: const fps = 30; const seconds = 5; <Composition fps={fps} durationInFrames={fps * seconds} .../>
Code Bad: <Composition fps={30} durationInFrames={90} .../> // 90 assumed to be 3s but silently wrong if fps changes to 60

Guideline: useCurrentFrame Is the Single Source of Truth for Time
Description: All motion must derive from useCurrentFrame(). Remotion renders each frame independently in a headless browser, so wall-clock time, setTimeout, and requestAnimationFrame do not exist during rendering and produce blank or frozen output.
Do: Read the frame from useCurrentFrame() and compute every animated value as a pure function of it
Don't: Drive animation with requestAnimationFrame, setInterval, or Date.now()
Code Good: const frame = useCurrentFrame(); const x = frame * 2; return <div style={{ transform: `translateX(${x}px)` }} />;
Code Bad: useEffect(() => { requestAnimationFrame(loop); }, []); // no-op during server-side frame capture — video renders static

Guideline: interpolate for Frame-Driven Value Mapping
Description: Use interpolate() to map the current frame to any numeric CSS or style value. Always pass extrapolateLeft/extrapolateRight: 'clamp' unless you deliberately want values to overshoot past the input range.
Do: Clamp interpolate() output so values never overshoot before or after the defined frame range
Don't: Leave extrapolate unset and let values shoot into negative or oversized ranges outside the animated window
Code Good: const opacity = interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 1], { extrapolateLeft: 'clamp', extrapolateRight: 'clamp' });
Code Bad: const opacity = interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 1]); // frame 60 gives opacity 2 — invalid CSS value

Guideline: spring() for Physics-Based Motion
Description: Use spring() instead of CSS easing curves for natural bounce and overshoot. spring() is deterministic given fps and frame, so it renders identically every time unlike CSS transitions which depend on real elapsed time.
Do: Drive bouncy or elastic motion with spring({ frame, fps, config })
Don't: Approximate spring motion with a cubic-bezier CSS transition — it depends on wall-clock time, not frame number
Code Good: const scale = spring({ frame, fps, config: { damping: 12, stiffness: 100 } });
Code Bad: style={{ transition: 'transform 0.5s cubic-bezier(.34,1.56,.64,1)' }} // driven by real time, not frame — breaks in rendered output

Guideline: Sequence for Time-Shifting Children
Description: Wrap a child component in <Sequence from={n} durationInFrames={m}> to delay its start and bound its lifetime. Inside a Sequence, useCurrentFrame() is automatically re-based to start at 0 for that child.
Do: Use <Sequence from={} durationInFrames={}> to time-shift and bound child components
Don't: Manually subtract an offset from the parent frame inside every child to fake sequencing
Code Good: <Sequence from={30} durationInFrames={60}><Title /></Sequence> // Title's useCurrentFrame() starts at 0 when parent frame hits 30
Code Bad: const frame = useCurrentFrame(); const localFrame = frame - 30; if (localFrame < 0) return null; // reimplements Sequence manually, error-prone

Guideline: AbsoluteFill for Full-Frame Layered Layouts
Description: Use <AbsoluteFill> to stack full-bleed layers (backgrounds, overlays, captions) without manually writing position:absolute, top:0, left:0, width:100%, height:100% on every layer.
Do: Stack full-canvas layers with <AbsoluteFill> and let flex props position content within each layer
Don't: Hand-write repetitive absolute positioning CSS for every full-frame layer
Code Good: <AbsoluteFill style={{ backgroundColor: 'black' }}><AbsoluteFill style={{ justifyContent: 'center' }}><Title /></AbsoluteFill></AbsoluteFill>
Code Bad:
...
// repeated on every layer

Guideline: staticFile for Assets in the public Folder
Description: Reference any bundled image, font, or audio file with staticFile('name.ext'), never a raw relative path. staticFile() resolves correctly both in the Studio dev server and in the headless render environment, where the working directory differs.
Do: Wrap every public/ asset reference in staticFile()
Don't: Use a bare relative path like './logo.png' for a public/ asset
Code Bad: // resolves relative to the wrong working directory during headless rendering

Guideline: Img and OffthreadVideo Instead of Native Tags
Description: Use Remotion's and components instead of native and
Do: Use and so Remotion waits for the asset before capturing the frame
Don't: Use a native or
Code Bad: // frame may be captured before the image decodes, producing a blank frame

Guideline: Audio Component for Sound with Volume Automation
Description: Add sound with <Audio src={...}>, and pass a function to the volume prop (frame => number) to fade or automate volume over time instead of a static number.
Do: Pass a frame-based function to the volume prop for fades and ducking
Don't: Try to control audio volume with imperative HTMLAudioElement.volume assignments in an effect
Code Good: <Audio src={staticFile('music.mp3')} volume={(f) => interpolate(f, [0, 30], [0, 1], { extrapolateLeft: 'clamp' })} />
Code Bad: useEffect(() => { audioRef.current.volume = 0.5; }, []); // imperative DOM audio API has no effect on headless frame rendering

Guideline: useVideoConfig Instead of Hardcoded Dimensions
Description: Read fps, width, height, and durationInFrames from useVideoConfig() inside components rather than hardcoding numbers. This keeps a component reusable across compositions with different resolutions or frame rates.
Do: Pull width/height/fps/durationInFrames from useVideoConfig() and compute layout relative to them
Don't: Hardcode pixel values or fps assumptions that only match one specific composition
Code Good: const { width, height, fps } = useVideoConfig(); const fontSize = height * 0.08;
Code Bad: const fontSize = 86; // only correct for a 1080p composition, breaks when reused at a different resolution

Guideline: delayRender/continueRender for Async Data Before Capture
Description: When a component needs to fetch data or wait on an async resource before it can render correctly, call delayRender() on mount and continueRender(handle) once the data resolves. Without this the frame is captured before the async work finishes.
Do: Call delayRender() before the async operation and continueRender(handle) in its resolution
Don't: Fetch data in a plain useEffect and rely on a re-render happening before the frame is captured
Code Good: const [handle] = useState(() => delayRender()); useEffect(() => { fetchData().then((d) => { setData(d); continueRender(handle); }); }, []);
Code Bad: useEffect(() => { fetchData().then(setData); }, []); // frame may be captured with data still null

Guideline: Zod Schema Plus defaultProps for Typed Inputs
Description: Define a zod schema and pass it to <Composition schema={...} defaultProps={...}>. This gives the Studio a typed, validated input-props editor and keeps renderMedia() calls (CLI or API) type-safe.
Do: Attach a zod schema and defaultProps to every Composition that takes input props
Don't: Type input props as `any` or leave the Composition without a schema, losing Studio validation
Code Good: const schema = z.object({ titleText: z.string() }); <Composition schema={schema} defaultProps={{ titleText: 'Hello' }} .../>
Code Bad: <Composition component={MyVideo} defaultProps={{ titleText: 'Hello' } as any} .../> // no validation, no Studio editor UI

Guideline: calculateMetadata for Dynamic Duration
Description: When a video's duration or dimensions depend on input props (e.g. number of slides, fetched data length), implement calculateMetadata on the Composition instead of a fixed durationInFrames.
Do: Return durationInFrames from calculateMetadata based on resolved props when length is data-dependent
Don't: Set a fixed durationInFrames and pad or truncate variable-length content to fit it
Code Good: calculateMetadata={async ({ props }) => ({ durationInFrames: props.slides.length * fps * 3 })}
Code Bad: durationInFrames={300} // fixed regardless of how many slides are actually passed in, cutting content off

Guideline: random() Instead of Math.random for Reproducible Output
Description: Use Remotion's random(seed) instead of Math.random(). Frames can be rendered out of order and in parallel across worker processes; Math.random() would produce different results per frame or per render, causing visible flicker or non-reproducible output.
Do: Seed randomness with Remotion's random(seed) so the same frame always produces the same value
Don't: Call Math.random() inside a component that renders per-frame during a parallelized render
Code Good: import { random } from 'remotion'; const jitter = random(`particle-${i}`) * 10;
Code Bad: const jitter = Math.random() * 10; // different value each render pass — visible flicker between frames rendered in parallel

Guideline: Components Must Be Pure Functions of the Frame
Description: A Remotion component must render the same output every time it is called with the same frame number. Do not mutate module-level state, accumulate values across renders, or rely on component lifecycle order — frames may render out of order or in separate processes.
Do: Compute every visual value purely from frame, props, and useVideoConfig — no accumulated or external mutable state
Don't: Increment a counter in module scope or a ref across renders to track 'how far the animation has gotten'
Code Good: const frame = useCurrentFrame(); const progress = frame / totalFrames; // pure function of frame
Code Bad: let globalProgress = 0; function MyVideo() { globalProgress += 0.01; return <div style={{ opacity: globalProgress }} />; } // depends on call order, breaks under parallel rendering

Guideline: No Real-Time CSS Transitions or Animations
Description: CSS transition and @keyframes animation both run on wall-clock time, which does not exist consistently across independently captured frames. Every animated property must instead be computed inline from useCurrentFrame() via interpolate() or spring().
Do: Compute animated style values inline from the current frame on every render
Don't: Rely on CSS `transition` or `animation` properties for any motion that must appear in the rendered video
Code Good: style={{ opacity: interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 1], { extrapolateLeft: 'clamp' }) }}
Code Bad: style={{ transition: 'opacity 1s' }} // headless frame capture takes a single snapshot per frame; CSS transition timing is irrelevant

Guideline: Player Component for Interactive Web Embeds
Description: Use @remotion/player's <Player> component to embed an interactive, scrubbable preview of a composition inside a regular React app (outside the Remotion Studio). It supports controls, autoPlay, loop, and is fully decoupled from server-side rendering.
Do: Embed <Player component={MyVideo} durationInFrames={} fps={} compositionWidth={} compositionHeight={} /> for in-app previews
Don't: Try to render Remotion compositions directly as normal React components outside Player and expect timeline scrubbing to work
Code Good: import { Player } from '@remotion/player'; <Player component={MyVideo} durationInFrames={150} fps={30} compositionWidth={1920} compositionHeight={1080} controls />
Code Bad: <MyVideo /> // renders once at frame 0 with no timeline, no scrubbing, no playback controls

Guideline: renderMedia/renderStill for Server-Side Output
Description: Use the @remotion/renderer Node.js APIs (renderMedia for video, renderStill for a single frame) or the `npx remotion render` CLI to produce final output files. These run in a headless Chromium instance separate from the interactive Studio/Player.
Do: Use renderMedia() or the CLI for producing final MP4/image output in a build or server pipeline
Don't: Try to export video by screen-recording the Player or Studio preview
Code Good: await renderMedia({ composition, serveUrl, codec: 'h264', outputLocation: 'out/video.mp4' });
Code Bad: // Screen-recording the browser preview loses frame-accurate timing, audio sync, and resolution fidelity

Guideline: Set Concurrency to Match Available CPU Cores
Description: renderMedia() renders frames in parallel across multiple headless browser tabs; concurrency defaults to roughly half the CPU core count. Raise it on render-farm machines with many cores, and lower it on memory-constrained containers where too many parallel Chromium tabs cause OOM crashes.
Do: Tune the concurrency option to the actual CPU/memory budget of the render environment
Don't: Leave concurrency at an arbitrary high fixed number that OOMs the render container
Code Good: await renderMedia({ ..., concurrency: os.cpus().length - 1 }); // scale to real core count
Code Bad: await renderMedia({ ..., concurrency: 32 }); // fixed value crashes a 4-core, 2GB render container

Guideline: Heavy Per-Frame Computation Must Be Memoized
Description: Every frame triggers a fresh render of the component tree. Expensive computation (parsing large datasets, generating paths, sorting) inside the render body runs once per frame, not once per composition — memoize it with useMemo keyed on the inputs that actually change.
Do: Wrap expensive derived data in useMemo so it only recomputes when its real dependencies change
Don't: Re-run expensive parsing or sorting logic directly in the component body on every frame
Code Good: const points = useMemo(() => computeChartPath(data), [data]);
Code Bad: const points = computeChartPath(data); // recalculated on every single frame of a 300-frame render

Guideline: @remotion/transitions for Cross-Sequence Transitions
Description: Use the @remotion/transitions package's <TransitionSeries> for fades, wipes, and slides between sequential scenes instead of hand-rolling opacity/transform overlap logic between adjacent <Sequence> components.
Do: Compose scene transitions with <TransitionSeries.Sequence> and a named presentation (fade, wipe, slide)
Don't: Manually overlap two <Sequence> ranges and hand-tune opacity crossfade math for every transition
Code Good: <TransitionSeries><TransitionSeries.Sequence durationInFrames={60}><SceneA /></TransitionSeries.Sequence><TransitionSeries.Transition presentation={fade()} timing={linearTiming({ durationInFrames: 20 })} /><TransitionSeries.Sequence durationInFrames={60}><SceneB /></TransitionSeries.Sequence></TransitionSeries>
Code Bad: // Hand-tuned overlapping Sequence ranges with manually interpolated crossfade opacity per scene pair

Guideline: @remotion/lottie for After Effects Animations
Description: Play Lottie/Bodymovin JSON exports (e.g. from After Effects) frame-accurately with the <Lottie> component from @remotion/lottie, which syncs playback to Remotion's frame number instead of real time.
Do: Use <Lottie animationData={} /> from @remotion/lottie so playback stays frame-synced with the rest of the composition
Don't: Embed a generic web Lottie player library that animates on its own internal real-time clock
Code Good: import { Lottie } from '@remotion/lottie'; <Lottie animationData={animationJson} />
Code Bad: import Lottie from 'lottie-react'; <Lottie animationData={animationJson} autoplay /> // plays on wall-clock time, desyncs from the rendered frame

Guideline: @remotion/captions for Auto-Generated Subtitles
Description: Use the @remotion/captions and @remotion/install-whisper-cpp packages to generate word-level timed caption data, then render captions as frame-driven text overlays instead of burning in a static subtitle track.
Do: Generate word-level caption timing data and drive caption visibility per-word from useCurrentFrame()
Don't: Hardcode subtitle text and timing by manually guessing frame ranges for each line
Code Good: const currentCaptions = getCurrentCaptions(captions, frame, fps); // per-frame lookup from generated timing data
Code Bad: <Sequence from={140}>{'Hardcoded subtitle line'}</Sequence> // manually guessed timing, drifts as content changes

Guideline: Wait for Fonts to Load Before Rendering
Description: Custom fonts must be fully loaded before a frame is captured, or text renders in a fallback font. Use @remotion/google-fonts for Google Fonts (which handles this automatically) or delayRender()/continueRender() around document.fonts.load() for self-hosted fonts.
Do: Use @remotion/google-fonts, or delay rendering until document.fonts.load() resolves for custom fonts
Don't: Assume a @font-face declaration is loaded by the time the first frame is captured
Code Good: import { loadFont } from '@remotion/google-fonts/Inter'; const { fontFamily } = loadFont();
Code Bad: // @font-face { font-family: 'Custom'; src: url(...) } with no load-wait — first frames render in the fallback font

Guideline: GPU Rendering Backend for WebGL/Canvas-Heavy Scenes
Description: Compositions using WebGL (Three.js, Skia) or heavy canvas drawing render significantly faster and more reliably with a hardware GPU backend (--gl=angle or a platform-specific flag) than with the default software rasterizer, and avoid GPU-driver crashes common on some Linux render hosts.
Do: Select an explicit --gl backend appropriate to the render host and test it before scaling out a render farm
Don't: Leave the OpenGL backend at its default on a Linux render host without verifying it handles the composition's WebGL content correctly
Code Good: npx remotion render MyComp out.mp4 --gl=angle
Code Bad: // default GL backend on a headless Linux worker silently produces black frames for a WebGL-heavy composition

Guideline: prefetch for Large Player Assets
Description: In an interactive <Player>, call prefetch() from 'remotion' for large videos or images before playback starts, so the browser has them cached instead of stalling the timeline on first access.
Do: Prefetch large media assets ahead of the moment they first appear in the Player timeline
Don't: Let the Player fetch a large video for the first time exactly when playback reaches its Sequence
Code Good: const { waitUntilDone } = prefetch(staticFile('background.mp4')); await waitUntilDone();
Code Bad: // No prefetch — Player stalls or shows a blank frame the instant playback reaches the video's Sequence

Guideline: Preview and Iterate with the Remotion Studio
Description: Run `npx remotion studio` during development to scrub the timeline, tweak input props live, and inspect each frame before committing to a full render. Full renders are comparatively slow; the Studio gives an immediate frame-accurate preview.
Do: Iterate on timing and layout in the Studio's scrubbable timeline before running a full render
Don't: Tune animation timing by repeatedly running full renderMedia() exports and eyeballing the output file
Code Good: npx remotion studio // live-reloading, scrubbable, frame-accurate preview during development
Code Bad: // Edit code -> full renderMedia() -> open output.mp4 -> repeat for every small timing tweak
